name: World Robot Summit Assembly Challenge
ability_definition: The ability to make precisely coordinated movements of the fingers of one or both hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects.

task_realism.reasoning: The task board uses real industrial small parts, such as M3 setscrews, M4 bolts, pulleys, bearings, belts and shafts. It requires insertion, fastening and assembly operations that closely mirror actual assembly-line and bench work, where human finger dexterity is exercised. The tasks are a somewhat curated, fixed-layout subset of real product assembly, but they are genuine manipulation-of-small-objects work.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Evaluation happens on physical hardware under time limits, with success-based scoring and some uncertainty in part placement, which is closer to real work than simulation. However, teams know the board in advance and heavily engineer their systems with custom tools, jigs and fixtures. They also get multiple tries in a competition setting. This differs from the variable, unstructured, sustained conditions of real workplace dexterity tasks.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The benchmark captures the 'assemble very small objects' and precision-insertion slice of the ability well. It largely misses precisely coordinated multi-finger movement, in-hand manipulation and bimanual finger coordination, because robots use parallel-jaw or custom grippers. Success can come from tooling and fixturing rather than dexterous control, so much of the construct is bypassed.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are real physical parts and outputs are physically assembled components scored on completion, which are authentic work artifacts. The standardized task board is a somewhat artificial arrangement compared with real product assemblies, but it is far from a toy or forced-choice format.

transferability_reasoning: The WRS Assembly Challenge is a physically grounded, realistic test of small-part precision assembly using genuine industrial components, which gives it strong realism and format fidelity. Transfer to human-like finger dexterity is limited because robots rely on grippers, custom tools and jigs instead of coordinated multi-finger control. Engineered, pre-known task conditions also inflate performance relative to variable real-world work.

2022.model_or_system: Top-scoring WRS 2020 team on the task-board task (team name not verified, so not given)
2022.metric: points (perfect score excluding time bonus = 100; this figure includes the time bonus)
2022.human_reference: Median manual assembly or production worker (specialist workforce that routinely handles small fasteners and parts by hand)
